arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Mills argued that the denial of summary judgment is not reviewable on appeal after a trial.
Mr. Mizer argued that the side that brought the case's main legal question relies on a false assumption about the nature of the appeal.

case.dek: The parties dispute whether federal appellate courts can review a district court's denial of summary judgment once a jury has decided the case.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of appellate review. the side that brought the case argues that a trial court's denial of summary judgment becomes unreviewable after a jury verdict. the opposing side contends that the appellate court retains the power to review that denial regardless of the trial outcome.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 25, lines 51-13

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 1, 2010.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-15

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Supreme Court to hold that appellate courts cannot review a summary judgment denial after a jury trial.
the opposing side wants the Supreme Court to hold that appellate courts can review a summary judgment denial even after a jury trial.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 25, lines 51-13

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that the denial of summary judgment is not reviewable on appeal after a trial has occurred.
the opposing side argues that the appellate court retains the power to review the denial of summary judgment regardless of the trial outcome.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts asked whether there is a difference between qualified immunity claims based on evidence and those based on law.
Justice Ginsburg asked how the standard for summary judgment differs from the standard applied after a trial concludes.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This dispute determines the finality of trial court decisions. It affects the ability of parties to challenge procedural rulings after a jury verdict. It shapes the scope of appellate review in federal civil cases. It impacts the efficiency of the judicial process. It influences the rights of litigants in civil disputes.
